'''''Dudleya virens''''', the '''green liveforever''' or '''bright green dudleya''', is an uncommon species of [[Perennial plant|perennial]], [[succulent plant]] in the family [[Crassulaceae]], native to several coastal southern [[California]] and [[Baja California]] locations.<ref>[http://www.calflora.org/cgi-bin/species_query.cgi?where-calrecnum=2870 Calflora Database: ''Dudleya virens''] . accessed 6.30.2013</ref>

==Distribution==
The succulent is found growing in the [[Palos Verdes Hills]] on the Palos Verdes Peninsula coast in [[Los Angeles County, California|Los Angeles County]]; on several of the [[Channel Islands (California)|Channel Islands]] in California; and on [[Guadalupe Island]] off the northwestern [[Baja California Peninsula]], Mexico.

==Description==
''Dudleya virens'' leaves are fleshy and strap-shaped, 8–20 cm long and 1.5–3 cm broad, tapering from the base (or from near middle) and are mostly green. They are arranged in a rosette.

The flowers are white, with five petals 7–10 mm long. They are produced in April, May, and June. Hummingbirds visit the flowers for their nectar.

There has been some developing arguments on how to best categorize the various subspecies of ''Dudleya virens''. The division stems from the fact that the current groupings of the ''Dudleya virens'' subspecies are polyphyletic as opposed to monophyletic.<ref name=":12">{{Cite journal |last=Yost |first=Jenn M. |last2=Bontrager |first2=Megan |last3=McCabe |first3=Stephen Ward |last4=Burton |first4=Darren |last5=Simpson |first5=Michael G. |last6=Kay |first6=Kathleen M. |last7=Ritter |first7=Matt |date=2013-12-01 |title=Phylogenetic Relationships and Evolution in Dudleya (Crassulaceae) |url=http://openurl.ingenta.com/content/xref?genre=article&issn=0363-6445&volume=38&issue=4&spage=1096 |journal=Systematic Botany |language=en |volume=38 |issue=4 |pages=1096–1104 |doi=10.1600/036364413X674760|url-access=subscription }}</ref> The overall evolutionary history of ''Dudleya virens'' has been difficult to pin down<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Amoroso |first=Danielle Marie |last2=Wilson |first2=Paul |date=2018-12-28 |title=Ten Cases of Divergence in the Seedling Ecology of Dudleya (Crassulaceae) |url=https://www.ingentaconnect.com/content/10.1600/036364418X697625 |journal=Systematic Botany |language=en |volume=43 |issue=4 |pages=889–900 |doi=10.1600/036364418X697625 |issn=0363-6445|url-access=subscription }}</ref> which has contributed to the confusion surrounding the clarification of the subspecies. This has led to some researchers suggesting that the white leafed sub species of should be separated into its own species that is distinct from the green colored subspecies, although this theory is not backed with any DNA results.<ref name=":12" />

==Cultivation==
''Dudleya virens'' is cultivated as an [[ornamental plant]] in the specialty [[native plant]]s and [[Succulent plant|succulent]]s [[horticulture]] trade.<ref>[http://www.rsabg.org/component/content/article?catid=162:native-gardening&id=681:coastal-gardens Rancho Santa Ana Botanic Garden: Native Plants for Coastal Gardens] {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20150924092331/http://www.rsabg.org/component/content/article?catid=162:native-gardening&id=681:coastal-gardens |date=2015-09-24 }} . accessed 6.30.2013</ref>  It is used in [[Container garden|containers]], [[xeriscape|drought tolerant landscapes]], and [[habitat garden]]s. It prefers well-draining soil, and grows best in full sun or light shade.

== Endangerment and Conservation ==

=== Poaching and predation ===
''Dudleya virens'' has been specifically affected by the surge in ''Dudleya'' poaching to be sold in a similar way to ''[[Dudleya farinosa]]'' which was covered in the 2021 documentary "[https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=qidgwbCPhNA Plant Heist]"<ref name=":22">{{Cite AV media |url=https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=qidgwbCPhNA |title=Plant Heist - Succulent Smuggling Documentary (SXSW Official selection) |date=2022-02-08 |last=Sibling Rivalry Creative |access-date=2024-12-11 |via=YouTube}}</ref>''.''  Where ''Dudleya virens'' plants are illegally harvested and shipped to regions of Asia to be sold for profit as medicine or as a pot plant.<ref name=":22" /> The succulent is also threatened by invasive grazing animal species that were introduced during the colonization of the Americas.<ref name=":02">{{Cite journal |last=McCabe |first=Stephen Ward |date=2024-03-11 |title=Dudleya of the Channel Islands: Conservation Successes and Taxonomy |url=https://bioone.org/journals/cactus-and-succulent-journal/volume-96/issue-1/015.096.0110/Dudleya-of-the-Channel-Islands-Conservation-Successes-and-Taxonomy/10.2985/015.096.0110.full |journal=Cactus and Succulent Journal |volume=96 |issue=1 |doi=10.2985/015.096.0110 |issn=0007-9367|url-access=subscription }}</ref> These animals over consume the plants.<ref name=":02" /> The poaching<ref name=":22" /> by people and predation<ref name=":02" /> by invasive species has led to ''Dudleya virens,'' specifically ''Dudleya virens'' spp. ''insularis,'' to be ranked a 1B.2 in terms of rarity (rare, threatened, or endangered) by the state of California.<ref name=":32">{{Cite web |last=Boudevin |first=Jesscia |date=2023-05-16 |title=Succulent Poaching a Problem - Catalina Island Conservancy |url=https://catalinaconservancy.org/stories/succulent-poaching-a-problem/#:~:text=these%20missing%20plants.%E2%80%9D-,Dudleya%20virens%20ssp.,;%20fairly%20threatened%20in%20California). |access-date=2024-12-11 |website=Catalina Island Conservancy - |language=en}}</ref>

=== Conservation ===
Through consorted conservation efforts, ''Dudleya virens'' has been able to make a considerable ecological come back from its previously concerning status.<ref name=":02" /> One of the major factors in their successful rehabilitation has been the removal of invasive grazing species: rabbits, horse, and pigs that were introduced during the colonization of California. These animals tend to over consume several ''Dudleya virens'' subspecies throughout the Channel Islands.<ref name=":02" /> The other major factor is that California passed a bill that makes poaching ''Dudleya virens'' with an intent to sell a fineable offense<ref name=":22" /><ref name=":32" />''.'' The removal of these invasive grazers and the crackdown on succulent poaching<ref name=":22" /><ref name=":02" /><ref name=":32" /> has created the conditions necessary for ''Dudleya virens'' to recover across the Channel Islands.<ref name=":02" />
